lessonTitle: Hallmarks of Cancer: Angiogenesis, Clonal Evolution and Heterogeneity

blocks.text: A woman with advanced lung cancer shrinks her tumour dramatically on a targeted drug, then relapses 14 months later with tumours that no longer respond. The relapsed cells were not new invaders; they were already present, a minority resistant clone waiting for the sensitive majority to be removed. Cancer is evolution at the scale of a single patient.

blocks.markdown: Cancers differ enormously, yet the cells share a small set of acquired capabilities, called the **hallmarks of cancer**. Each is acquired through mutations or epigenetic changes in genes that control growth, death and tissue behaviour: **oncogenes** (gain of function, one allele is enough) and **tumour suppressor genes** (loss of function, usually both alleles must be lost).

blocks.title: Hallmarks of cancer
blocks.text: The hallmarks are functional capabilities that a clone acquires as it progresses from a normal cell to a malignancy: sustaining proliferative signalling, evading growth suppressors, resisting cell death, enabling replicative immortality, inducing angiogenesis, and activating invasion and metastasis. Two further hallmarks are reprogrammed energy metabolism and evasion of immune destruction. Genome instability and tumour-promoting inflammation are enabling characteristics that speed acquisition.

rows: Activating mutation of an oncogene such as RAS, or amplification of a growth factor receptor
Loss of RB or TP53 function removes cell cycle brakes
Overexpression of BCL-2 blocks mitochondrial apoptosis
Telomerase reactivation maintains telomere length so cells divide indefinitely
Hypoxia-driven release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
Loss of E-cadherin, protease secretion, entry into lymphatics or blood
Aerobic glycolysis (Warburg effect): high glucose uptake even when oxygen is available
Checkpoint ligand expression such as PD-L1, loss of antigen presentation
blocks.caption: Hallmarks with a representative mechanism each.

blocks.markdown: **Tumour angiogenesis.** Oxygen and nutrients reach cells by diffusion over only about 100 to 200 micrometres, so a tumour without its own blood supply stays at about 1 to 2 mm in diameter. Growth beyond this requires the **angiogenic switch**: hypoxic tumour cells stabilise hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1), which drives transcription of **VEGF**. VEGF binds receptors on endothelial cells (VEGFR-2), causing sprouting of new vessels. Tumour vessels are disorganised and leaky, which raises interstitial pressure and limits drug delivery.

Angiogenesis is targeted by **bevacizumab**, a monoclonal antibody against VEGF-A, and by tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as sunitinib that block VEGF receptors. Because VEGF also maintains normal endothelium, class adverse effects include hypertension, proteinuria, bleeding, thrombosis, impaired wound healing and, rarely, gastrointestinal perforation.

blocks.caption: N is the number of cells after n doublings from one cell; T_d is the doubling time; t is the elapsed time.

blocks.title: How long does a tumour take to reach a detectable size?
blocks.prompt: A tumour cell population doubles every 50 days. Starting from one transformed cell, estimate the time to reach about one million (10^6) cells.

steps.text: Find the number of doublings n from 2^n equals 10^6.
Round to about 20 doublings (2^20 is just over one million).

blocks.answer: About 20 doublings, so roughly 1000 days (2.7 years) to reach a million cells; clinical detection needs about 10^9 cells, so most of a tumour's life is silent.

rows: VEGF dominates after the angiogenic switch
blocks.caption: Tumour versus normal vasculature.

blocks.markdown: **Clonal evolution and heterogeneity.** A tumour arises from one cell, but mutations accumulate during divisions, creating subclones. Mutations present in every cancer cell (**truncal**) arose early; those present in only some cells (**subclonal**) arose later. Selection acts on this variation: a therapy that kills sensitive cells favours any pre-existing resistant subclone, which then expands. This explains **intratumour heterogeneity** and relapse after initially successful treatment.

Sequencing estimates how common a mutation is using the **variant allele fraction (VAF)**, the fraction of sequencing reads carrying the mutation. Assuming a diploid genome without copy-number change, a heterozygous mutation in every tumour cell has VAF equal to half the tumour purity p (the fraction of cells that are cancer cells).

blocks.caption: f is the fraction of tumour cells carrying a heterozygous mutation; f = 1 means clonal.

blocks.title: Is this mutation clonal or subclonal?
blocks.prompt: A biopsy has tumour purity p = 0.80. A KRAS mutation has VAF 0.40 and a second mutation has VAF 0.12. Calculate the fraction of tumour cells carrying each.

steps.text: f = 1 means every tumour cell carries it (truncal); f = 0.30 means only 30% do (subclonal).

blocks.answer: KRAS is clonal (all tumour cells) and the second mutation is subclonal (30% of tumour cells).

blocks.title: Hallmarks and therapy
blocks.text: Each hallmark suggests a therapeutic target, and tumour heterogeneity explains why single-agent targeted therapy so often fails: a rare resistant subclone survives and regrows.

points: The hallmarks are acquired capabilities driven by oncogene activation and tumour suppressor loss, with genome instability and inflammation as enabling characteristics.
Tumours beyond about 1 to 2 mm need the HIF-1 and VEGF driven angiogenic switch; anti-VEGF agents such as bevacizumab cause hypertension, proteinuria and bleeding.
Clonal evolution creates truncal and subclonal mutations; selection by therapy expands resistant subclones.

questions.stem: A follicular lymphoma carries t(14;18), which places BCL-2 under an immunoglobulin promoter. Which hallmark does this primarily support?

options.text: Resisting cell death
Inducing angiogenesis
Activating invasion
Enabling replicative immortality

distractorRationale.c: Invasion involves loss of adhesion and proteases.

questions.explanation: BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein; its overexpression lets cells survive signals that would normally trigger apoptosis. The result is accumulation of cells rather than faster division.

questions.stem: Cells from a tumour continue dividing after more than 100 passages in culture whereas normal fibroblasts stop after about 50. Telomerase is strongly expressed in the tumour cells. Which hallmark is this?

options.text: Enabling replicative immortality
Evading growth suppressors by RB loss
Sustained proliferative signalling by receptor mutation
Tumour-promoting inflammation

distractorRationale.b: RB loss is a separate mechanism.
distractorRationale.c: Receptor mutation is a signalling mechanism, not telomere maintenance.

questions.explanation: Normal cells lose telomere length at each division until they senesce. Telomerase reactivation prevents this, allowing unlimited division.

questions.stem: What drives the angiogenic switch in a growing tumour?

options.text: Hypoxia stabilising HIF-1 and increasing VEGF production
Excess oxygen delivery
Loss of VEGF receptors on endothelium
Direct conversion of tumour cells to red cells

questions.correctOptionText: Hypoxia stabilising HIF-1 and increasing VEGF production

distractorRationale.b: Hypoxia, not excess oxygen, triggers it.
distractorRationale.c: Receptors are required for VEGF signalling.
distractorRationale.d: Tumour cells do not become red cells.

questions.explanation: Diffusion limits the size of an avascular tumour. Hypoxic cells stabilise HIF-1, which increases VEGF and recruits new vessels.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with metastatic colorectal cancer receives bevacizumab and develops a blood pressure of 168/98 mmHg and proteinuria. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Inhibiting VEGF impairs normal endothelial function
The drug is a cytotoxic antimetabolite causing myelosuppression
The drug blocks the epidermal growth factor receptor
The tumour has become a hormone-secreting tumour

questions.correctOptionText: Inhibiting VEGF impairs normal endothelial function

distractorRationale.a: Correct: VEGF maintains normal endothelium and glomerular function.
distractorRationale.b: Bevacizumab is a monoclonal antibody, not an antimetabolite.
distractorRationale.c: EGFR blockade causes rash, not this picture.

questions.explanation: VEGF supports nitric oxide production and glomerular endothelium, so its blockade causes hypertension and proteinuria. These class effects require monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient's tumour relapses after initially responding to a targeted drug. Resistant cells are found at 2% frequency in a pre-treatment sample. Which process best explains relapse?

options.text: Selection and expansion of a pre-existing resistant subclone
Drug-induced conversion of all cells to the resistant state in a day
Loss of tumour heterogeneity
Immediate angiogenesis from drug exposure

questions.correctOptionText: Selection and expansion of a pre-existing resistant subclone

distractorRationale.a: Correct: therapy removes sensitive cells and resistant cells expand.
distractorRationale.b: Resistance usually pre-exists or arises by mutation, not instantly in all cells.
distractorRationale.c: Heterogeneity is the cause, not lost.

questions.explanation: Therapy provides selective pressure. A resistant subclone that was present at low frequency survives and repopulates the tumour.

questions.stem: A truncal mutation is one present in all tumour cells because it arose early in the clonal history.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Truncal mutations are shared by all descendants of the founding clone. Subclonal mutations arise later and are found in only part of the tumour.

questions.stem: A tumour doubles every 80 days. Estimate how many days are needed to grow from one cell to 10^9 cells (use the number of doublings n = log2 of 10^9, about 30). Give your answer in days.
questions.explanation: The number of doublings is log2(10^9), about 29.9, so about 30. Multiply by 80 days to get about 2400 days, around 6.6 years, showing that tumours are silent for years before detection.

questions.stem: A tumour sample has purity 0.50. A heterozygous mutation has VAF 0.10 (diploid, no copy-number change). Calculate the fraction of tumour cells carrying the mutation (dimensionless, 0 to 1).
questions.explanation: Using f = 2 VAF / p, f = 2 times 0.10 divided by 0.50, which is 0.40. The mutation is subclonal because f is less than 1.

questions.stem: Choose three hallmarks of cancer and, for each, explain the molecular mechanism by which a cell acquires it. Give a named gene or protein in each case.
markingGuide: Evading growth suppressors: loss of RB or TP53
Resisting death: BCL-2 overexpression or TP53 loss
Proliferative signalling: RAS or receptor activation
Distinguish oncogene gain of function from suppressor loss
questions.explanation: Each hallmark must be tied to a specific molecular event. Credit should be given for linking mechanism to cellular behaviour.

questions.stem: Explain the angiogenic switch and why anti-VEGF therapy is used in solid tumours. Describe two adverse effects and the mechanism of each.
markingGuide: Diffusion limit of about 100 to 200 micrometres restricts avascular tumour size
Hypoxia stabilises HIF-1, which increases VEGF
VEGF stimulates endothelial sprouting through VEGFR
Tumour vessels are leaky and disorganised
Bevacizumab binds VEGF-A or TKIs block receptors
Hypertension from reduced nitric oxide and endothelial function
Proteinuria, bleeding or impaired wound healing with mechanism
questions.explanation: Anti-VEGF therapy starves or prunes tumour vessels, but VEGF also maintains normal vessels. Marking should link each adverse effect to normal VEGF function.
